title: Develop Capabilities: Digital Certificates
summary: This sub-technique covers an adversary generating their own self-signed SSL/TLS (Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security) certificates while building out infrastructure, before any victim is touched. The attacker runs a key generation and certificate signing tool, so the same private key that the certificate describes is also the key that signs the certificate. The resulting files contain a public key, a subject identity, and a signature made without approval from any external certificate authority. Because no authority vouches for it, browsers and clients raise trust errors unless the certificate is manually trusted or a root certificate is installed on the target. Operators use these certificates to encrypt command and control channels over web protocols, to give malicious login pages a padlock, or to support adversary-in-the-middle interception of traffic. The defensible artefacts are the certificate itself plus its fingerprint: a self-signed issuer equal to the subject, generic or oddly specific common names, very short validity windows, unusual serial numbers, and the absence of any certificate transparency entry. Legitimate public services validate their identity with a third-party authority, so anything terminating in an unknown self-signed root that is not part of a managed internal public key infrastructure is worth flagging. Detection is mainly network, passive DNS, and internet scanning rather than endpoint telemetry, because the work happens on adversary-controlled systems.

beginner.definition: A digital certificate is like an identity card for a website or a server. Normally a trusted company signs that card to confirm the owner is real. Self-signing means an attacker creates the card and signs it themselves, so nobody independent checks it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers want their malicious servers to look normal and encrypted. A self-made certificate lets them do that without paying for or proving a real identity. If nobody looks closely, users may trust a harmful site. Security tools may warn loudly instead, which is useful for you as a defender.
howItWorks: The attacker creates a private key (a secret number) and a matching public key.
They enter details such as a company name and a domain to describe the certificate owner.
They sign the certificate with their own key instead of sending it to a certificate authority.
Because the signer is unknown, browsers and clients show a trust warning by default.
They use the certificate to encrypt traffic or make a fake site look secure.
If they can add it to a victim's trusted list, the warnings disappear.
beginner.example: Think of a nightclub with a guest list. A real club checks your passport before letting you in. That passport is printed by a government, so the club trusts it. A self-signed certificate is like printing your own passport at home. The photo and name look fine, and you can wave it at the door. The bouncer only accepts it if he already decided to trust your home printer, and most bouncers will not.
takeaways: Encrypted traffic is not the same as trusted traffic.
Self-signed certificates on internet-facing servers are common in attacker infrastructure.
Always check who issued a certificate before you trust it.

objectives: Explain what a self-signed certificate is and why no third party vouches for it.
Describe how an adversary uses a self-signed certificate to encrypt command and control traffic.
Identify the certificate fields that help a defender link adversary infrastructure together.
Tell the difference between attacker self-signed certificates and managed internal certificates.
Name the log or data source that reveals a newly seen certificate on your network.
